reader_notes: Read from /tmp/claude-0/sp/gold/aof06.txt. Entries found with a scripted search that sampled the sounding pitch at the subject's template onsets (normal, diminished and augmented; upright and inverted; head a fourth or fifth). Each hit and every cadence was then checked by reading the passage and the vertical sonorities. Beats are half notes (2/2). The subject is D A G F E D C# D E F G F E D (4 bars normal, 2 bars diminished); the inverted form on A is A D E F G A Bb A G F E F G A. Degrees are Roman numerals from D minor (v = A minor). stretto_with follows the protocol literally (begins strictly before the earlier entry's midpoint); several entries begin exactly at a midpoint and are marked so in their reason.

cadences.reason: E7 at 10:1 (bass E3, G#4 in the alto) resolves to an F-major chord (bass F3) at 10:2, where the soprano's diminished subject in A minor enters.
V (E3 in bass, C5 suspension) to i at 12:1: the bass drops out and the tenor takes A3; soprano rises to C5 (^3). Closes the exposition and its dominant pair; the tirata episode follows.

A7 at 15:1 (soprano G5, tenor C#4) to d at 15:1.5 with the soprano on F5 (^3) and an E5 suspension in the alto. The bass's A3-D3 is the head of its own inverted entry, so the cadence is elided into the new group. Unsure whether to count it as a phrase close.
C7/E (bass E3, alto Bb4) to F at 26:1, soprano on F4; first inversion dominant, so imperfect. Soprano rests after it; the tenor's diminished inversion starts on the arrival.

The alto's F-major entry ends on F4 at 29:1, but the bass goes E3-D3 under C/E, giving a D-minor chord (vi) that starts the descending-fifths sequence. Unsure: the dominant is inverted, and this may be better heard as no cadence.
The dominant pedal A2 (31:2-33:1) with C#3 in the tenor resolves to Bb2/D3: a Bb chord (VI) at 33:2, which turns the music toward G minor.
D7/A (bass A2, C5, F#4) to g at 38:1, soprano Bb4 (^3). The alto drops out here, but the arrival falls inside the soprano's inverted statement (index 9), so the close is weak. Unsure.

Bb (46:1), then a diminished chord over Bb3, then A7 at 46:2. The upper voices resolve to d at 46:2.5 while the bass rests, and the bass re-enters on A2 with the inverted subject at 47:1 instead of supplying the tonic.

Three-voice passage (bass resting): A7 with Bb4 at 55:2, then A at 55:2.5, to d at 56:1 with the tenor's run A3-D3 as bass and the soprano on F4 (^3). Lightly marked: the soprano at once starts a rising chromatic line to the 57:1 entry.
A7 (C#3 at 60:2, then a sixteenth-note descent from A3) to D3 at 61:1. The top sounding voice (alto, soprano resting) is on F4 (^3), and the tenor's altered diminished subject closes on D4.

Bb2 (68:1) and G2 lead to F#2 under D and A: V6 of g at 68:2, where the soprano's inversion ends on A4. The bass rests and the upper voices move to g at 69:1, starting the closing sequence. Arrival on an inverted V, so it is a weak HC.

A7/C# at 73:1, then a general pause (all voices rest at 73:1.5), then a French-overture upbeat (A2, C#5, tirata in the soprano) to D3 at 73:2 with the soprano on F5 (^3), descending to D5 at 73:2.5. A dramatic cadence that the following bar confirms.

Cadential 6/4 (d/A at 74:1), V (A, C#5) at 74:1.5, then I at 74:2 on D3 with the soprano on D5; the alto's G4 suspension resolves to F#4 (major third). The bass holds this D to the end: the tonic pedal.

Not one of the protocol's kinds. Over the tonic pedal, D7 to g (77-78), then an E-G sonority, to a D-major chord at 79:2 (tierce de Picardie). The dominant-to-tonic close was already made at 74:2; this is the final plagal close.

sections.name: exposition
sections.notes: Stretto exposition by inversion and diminution: bass (normal, 1:1), soprano (inverted, diminished, 2:1), alto (diminished, 3:2), tenor (inverted, diminished, tonal, in a, 7:1). Bars 5-6 are a free codetta (bass dotted scales). It continues with an extra pair in the dominant (alto normal 8:1, soprano diminished 10:2), then a deceptive cadence (10:2) and an IAC in a (12:1).

countersubject.notes: No regular countersubject. The counterpoint to each statement is mostly another statement of the subject in a different form: upright against inverted, normal against diminished (e.g. 1:1+2:1, 16:1+16:2, 31:1+32:1, 47:1+48:1, 58:1+58:2, 64:2+65:2). Free voices use recurring stock figures (dotted scale runs, thirty-second-note tiratas, sixteenth-note runs) that do not form a fixed line.

31:2-33:2, dominant pedal under the tenor subject and alto inversion; resolves deceptively to Bb2.
74:2 to the end; tonic pedal under the two last entries (in g) and the plagal close.

notes: Counter-fugue in the French style: there are no augmentations here (augmentation belongs to VII), only normal and half values, upright and inverted. 28 entries in all: 18 in diminution, 10 in normal values, 13 inverted. Twice the subject appears with a shrunken head, a fourth instead of a fifth (soprano 57:1 E-A, tenor 74:2 A-D); with the exposition's tenor answer (7:1 D-A for E-A) these are the only tonally adjusted forms. Other statements are exact or alter one note at index 6 or 12 to tonicize (20:2 B natural, 26:1 Db, 31:1 Eb, 42:1 E natural). Alto 47:1 (E4 A4 G4 F4 E4 D4 C#4 D4, then free) is a head-fragment anticipating the tenor's diminished subject at 48:1. It is not counted as an entry: it continues from the alto's previous line without a rest. The A2 at 33:1.75, the C3 held 34:2-35:2 under the soprano's g-minor entry, and the D3 held 67:1-67:2.6 are short sustained bass notes, not listed as pedals. The general pause at 73:1.5 and the following dotted upbeat to 73:2 are a deliberate French-overture gesture before the final cadences. The piece ends on a D-major chord (tierce de Picardie). Unsure: whether 15:1.5, 29:1, 38:1 and 56:1 count as phrase-closing cadences; the label 'answer' for 57:1 and 74:2; the section boundaries 8-12 (extra dominant pair, kept in the exposition) and 44-47 (episode, starting from F, the arrival of the alto's Bb entry).
